prompt: Design an account settings page for Marlowe Cloud, a file-sync app. It has three sections: Profile (display name, email, time zone), Notifications (email digest, mobile push, mention alerts, weekly summary) and Privacy (profile visibility, activity status, data export). Show each setting with its label, a short description where useful, and a suitable control. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets or scripts. The important content must be visible in the first 1280x800 viewport.
rubric: Space inside each section is clearly smaller than the space between sections, so three groups are visible at a glance.
Each section heading sits visibly closer to its own settings than to the section above it.
Sections are separated mainly by space and headings, not by a bordered or shadowed box around every group.
Padding and gaps look like they come from a small consistent set of values rather than many near-duplicates.
Labels, descriptions and controls share a common left edge, and each label sits close to its own control.

prompt: Design a 'What you get' section for Keyhollow, a password manager. It lists six features, each with a short title and one sentence: autofill across devices, breach alerts, secure sharing with family, an offline vault, passkey support and emergency access. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets or scripts. The important content must be visible in the first 1280x800 viewport.
rubric: The six features are not presented as six identical bordered cards with icon circles unless the page gives a clear reason for cards.
Within each feature the title sits close to its sentence, and the gap between features is clearly larger.
The section feels comfortable, neither cramped nor mostly empty, with a visible gap above and below it.
The features line up on shared edges and the columns or rows have a consistent rhythm.
Spacing values appear systematic rather than arbitrary.

prompt: Our analytics dashboard has one large panel that works as a card (border, soft shadow, 24px padding). Inside it are three smaller cards, each with its own border, shadow and 24px padding, with 8px gaps between them. Section headings inside the panel have 16px above and 16px below. The page looks heavy and the groups are hard to tell apart. What would you change? Keep it practical.
rubric: Identifies the nested surfaces and proposes flattening them, for example by keeping one container or dropping the inner borders and shadows.
Notes that the 8px gaps are smaller than the 24px padding, which blurs grouping, and proposes gaps that are at least as large as the padding or a different separation.
Proposes more space above each section heading than below it so the heading attaches to its content.
Suggests reducing the doubled borders and shadows rather than only changing sizes.
Gives concrete replacement values or a clear target rather than only general advice.
Replaces bottom and right margins on children with spacing owned by the parent container, such as gap.
Normalizes the one-off values (13px, 22px, 7px, 19px and the like) to a small set of consistent steps.
Makes the card padding consistent, including the featured card, unless it explains a reason for a difference.
Removes the doubled gap that appears after the last item in a group.
Gives the buttons more comfortable padding, with horizontal padding larger than vertical.

prompt: We are building a notifications list for a project tool. It has about 30 items, and each shows a title, a time and a small action button. Should we separate the items with dividers, with cards, or with space only? Answer in under 120 words.
rubric: Recommends dividers or space only for a long, scannable list rather than cards on every item.
Gives a reason based on density, scanning or visual weight.
Mentions keeping enough space between the small action buttons so they are easy to tap or click.
Stays under about 120 words and commits to one recommendation.

prompt: Explain to a front-end developer why the team uses a fixed spacing scale instead of choosing values by eye for each component. Answer in under 120 words.
rubric: States that the same relationship gets the same space everywhere, so the product looks consistent.
Mentions that fewer decisions are needed or that choices are faster.
Mentions easier maintenance, such as changing a step in one place.
Says the scale has a small number of steps rather than many.
Stays under about 120 words and is written plainly.

prompt: Our analytics tool needs a compact mode for power users who live in it all day and a comfortable mode for people who open it once a week. Describe how spacing should change between the two modes, using concrete values where helpful. Keep it practical for an engineer to implement.
rubric: Compresses the spacing steps in compact mode while keeping groups visibly separate, so within-group space stays smaller than between-group space.
Keeps a readable minimum text size in compact mode instead of shrinking type to gain density.
Addresses target size or spacing for clicking or tapping, especially for any touch use.
Keeps the structure and order of content the same in both modes, changing only spacing and sizes.
Suggests implementing the modes with shared variables or tokens rather than rewriting each component.

prompt: Design a gig poster for a jazz night called Blue Lantern Sessions. Include the band name (The Harbour Quartet), the date (Friday 14 November), the venue (The Copper Room, 22 Mill Street) and the ticket price ($15 at the door). Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets or scripts. The important content must be visible in the first 1280x800 viewport.
rubric: The composition is expressive, with strong contrast in scale between the band or event name and the supporting details.
The date, venue and price are legible and easy to find.
Spacing is intentional and varied for effect rather than uniform padding between evenly boxed blocks.
The poster is not built as interface-style cards or a form-like stack of equally padded sections.

prompt: Build a stock watchlist table for a trading app with 25 rows visible at once in the first screen. Columns: symbol, company name, last price, change, change percent, volume. Use made-up but plausible tickers and numbers. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets or scripts. The important content must be visible in the first 1280x800 viewport.
rubric: Rows are compact enough that about 25 rows are visible in the first viewport.
The table stays readable through alignment, with numbers right-aligned and consistent columns.
Rows are separated by subtle rules or light banding rather than by heavy boxes or large gaps.
The rows are not padded out to a comfortable or marketing-style density.
Text remains at a legible size and does not shrink to tiny type to fit the rows.

prompt: Our team's kanban board shows each task as a card with a border and a soft shadow, and people drag tasks between columns. A reviewer says cards are overused in the product and that we should use plain space instead. Is that right for this board? Advise briefly.
rubric: Defends keeping cards on this board because tasks are discrete objects that people drag and act on.
Recommends keeping the card surface consistent across tasks and quiet rather than heavy.
May suggest dropping either the border or the shadow so a card does not carry both.
Does not recommend removing the cards wholesale.
Can still point out places where space would serve better than extra boxes, such as inside a card or around column headers.
